\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

All eight generators are base (pretrained) models.
This is a deliberate design choice: base models isolate the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects, enabling controlled study of recursive distributional drift.
However, web text is predominantly produced by instruction-tuned and RLHF-aligned models.
Preliminary instruct experiments confirm that depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct drops to LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.763 base) and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template to 0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 under a 7-generator split).
Length-matched analysis yields near-zero correlations ($|\rho| < 0.02$) and binary classification near chance (F1\,$\approx$\,0.5) for Qwen models, leaving interpretation ambiguous.
Extending depth fingerprinting to instruct models requires addressing these confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping) that instruction tuning introduces.

Our experiments include generators up to 8.2B parameters (Qwen3-8B).
Depth signal persists at this scale (Qwen3-8B 3-class F1\,=\,0.714), but cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap vs.\ $\leq$2.8B generators (F1\,=\,0.77--0.81).
Frontier models (70B+) remain untested; their higher fluency may further compress feature margins.

Differential depth response strength is prompt-type dependent: within-type 3-class F1 ranges from 0.78 (continuation) to 0.73 (elaboration), with inspired rewriting intermediate at 0.74 (Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}).
DDR is most reliably detected in continuation-style generation; near-paraphrastic settings approach the method's detection floor.
Cross-prompt-type transfer (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753) confirms shared signal, yet additional prompt types (e.g., summarization, instruction following) and cross-generator $\times$ cross-prompt interactions remain untested.

Our primary evaluation uses single-generator chains; cross-model chains (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}) confirm depth signal under generator heterogeneity (3-class F1\,=\,0.789, binary F1\,=\,0.830; evaluated on the 5-generator subset for which cross-model chains were available), though these generators represent a controlled laboratory setting rather than the full diversity of real-world contamination.
Simulated human editing (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) suggests graceful degradation, but the gap between simulated token replacement and real-world post-processing remains untested.
Independent gen-0 seed sets per generator would eliminate potential memorization effects in 3-class LOGO evaluation; we report leak-free binary F1 as the primary metric to mitigate this limitation.

The reference model is fixed to Pythia-410M throughout, although cross-family reference experiments (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) confirm the phenomenon is not reference-specific (spread 0.013 across three references).
All seed texts in the main evaluation are English Wikipedia excerpts.
Cross-domain evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:domain}) shows that depth signal persists across News, Academic, and Code domains (binary F1 $>$ 0.73 under LOGO at $t{=}1.0$), though a domain $\times$ temperature interaction exists: certain domain/generator combinations at lower temperature approach chance level (e.g., Academic domain binary F1\,=\,0.628 at $t{=}0.7$), suggesting that reference model calibration is critical for cross-domain deployment.
The reference model dependency (Pythia-410M, English-centric pretraining) limits non-English applicability and adds inference overhead relative to surface-feature-only approaches.
Generalization to other languages remains untested.

Our default analysis uses fixed decoding parameters (temperature 0.7, nucleus $p{=}0.9$). A sampling ablation (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}) shows robustness to moderate variation ($t \in [0.5, 0.7]$, ${\leq}0.3$\,pp) but substantial degradation at $t{=}1.0$ ($-6$\,pp), indicating that depth fingerprinting assumes standard decoding regimes.
Cross-temperature transfer shows substantial degradation when test-time temperature exceeds training-time settings, limiting deployment to scenarios where the generation temperature is approximately known.

We use 3-class granularity (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+). A 5-class evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}) yields LOGO F1\,$\approx$\,0.50, with depths 2--4 mutually indistinguishable, validating the 3-class design as the practical resolution limit.

To verify that the depth signal resides in the features rather than the classifier,
we repeat the 6-generator LOGO evaluation using Logistic Regression and Random Forest
in place of XGBoost (Table~\ref{tab:alt-classifier}).
All other settings (the same 7 features, 3-class labels, and class-balanced downsampling) are
kept identical. For Logistic Regression we apply standard scaling to the features.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{LOGO macro-F1 across three classifiers. Each column shows the held-out generator F1. (6-generator LOGO; 3-class.)}
\label{tab:alt-classifier}
\small
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{lc cccccc}
\toprule
Classifier & Avg F1 & OLMo-2 & Py-1B & Py-2.8B & Qw-0.6B & Qw-1.7B & Qw-8B \\
\midrule
XGBoost          & 0.789 & 0.764 & 0.856 & 0.804 & 0.824 & 0.806 & 0.683 \\
Random Forest    & 0.790 & 0.764 & 0.856 & 0.804 & 0.825 & 0.807 & 0.684 \\
Logistic Regr.   & 0.725 & 0.719 & 0.781 & 0.740 & 0.745 & 0.743 & 0.624 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

Both tree-based classifiers achieve LOGO F1 $\approx 0.79$,
and even a linear model reaches $0.725$, well above the $0.33$ chance baseline for
three classes.
The per-generator ranking is also consistent across classifiers
(Pythia-1B easiest, Qwen3-8B hardest),
confirming that discriminative power originates in the entropy and lexical features,
not in classifier capacity.
Ordinal-specific methods (CORAL \cite{coral_ordinal}, Frank-Hall \cite{frank_hall_ordinal}) achieve comparable F1 with overlapping CIs, which confirms that 3-class granularity provides insufficient resolution for ranking-aware losses to improve over standard multiclass classification.

\subsection*{Sampling Sensitivity Analysis}
\label{app:sampling-sensitivity}

To assess robustness to decoding temperature, we regenerate continuation chains at $t \in \{0.5, 0.9\}$ with fixed nucleus $p{=}0.9$ (matching the default) for four generators spanning three model families: Pythia-2.8B, OLMo-2-1B, Qwen3-1.7B, and Qwen3-0.6B (Table~\ref{tab:sampling-ablation}).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Depth classification under varying temperature (fixed top-$p$\,=\,0.9). Binary: gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+. LOGO evaluation; 95\% bootstrap CIs.$^{\ast}$$^{\dagger}$}

\section{9-Generator Scale Evaluation}\label{app:9gen-scale}

This analysis extends the main 8-generator LOGO evaluation (Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}) to nine generators by adding Gemma-2-2B, a model from a previously unrepresented architecture family (Gemma).
Table~\ref{tab:9gen-logo} reports per-generator LOGO performance under this expanded set.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{9-generator LOGO evaluation. Each row holds out the listed generator at test time. 3-class: gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+; binary: gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+. 95\% bootstrap CIs in brackets.}
\label{tab:9gen-logo}
\small
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{llr cc cc}
\toprule
\textbf{Generator} & \textbf{Family} & \textbf{Params} & \textbf{3-class F1} & \textbf{95\% CI} & \textbf{Binary F1} & \textbf{95\% CI} \\
\midrule
Pythia-1B       & Pythia  & 1.0B & 0.857 & [0.848, 0.866] & 0.785 & --- \\
Qwen3-0.6B      & Qwen    & 0.6B & 0.819 & [0.807, 0.830] & 0.743 & --- \\
Pythia-2.8B     & Pythia  & 2.8B & 0.812 & [0.801, 0.822] & 0.728 & --- \\
Qwen3-1.7B      & Qwen    & 1.7B & 0.811 & [0.800, 0.823] & 0.746 & --- \\
OLMo-2-1B       & OLMo    & 1.5B & 0.773 & [0.762, 0.784] & 0.692 & --- \\
Llama-3.2-3B    & Llama   & 3.2B & 0.759 & [0.748, 0.770] & 0.680 & --- \\
Qwen3-8B        & Qwen    & 8.2B & 0.696 & [0.683, 0.709] & 0.647 & [0.638, 0.671] \\
Gemma-2-2B      & Gemma   & 2.6B & 0.628 & [0.622, 0.634] & 0.440 & [0.432, 0.449] \\
Mistral-7B      & Mistral & 7.0B & 0.605 & [0.593, 0.617] & 0.534 & --- \\
\midrule
\textbf{Average (9-gen)} & & & \textbf{0.751} & & \textbf{0.666} & \\
\textbf{Average (8-gen)} & & & \textbf{0.770} & & \textbf{0.694} & \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Overall comparison.}
Adding Gemma-2-2B reduces the mean 3-class LOGO F1 from 0.770 (8-gen) to 0.751 (9-gen), a drop of $\Delta = -0.019$.
The per-generator F1 values for the original eight generators shift by at most $[-0.011, +0.002]$, indicating that the inclusion of Gemma data in training does not destabilize existing generalization patterns.

\paragraph{Gemma-2-2B anomaly.}
Gemma-2-2B is the weakest held-out generator: 3-class F1\,=\,0.628, binary F1\,=\,0.440.
Per-class breakdown reveals a striking asymmetry: gen-0 F1\,=\,0.991 and gen-2+ F1\,=\,0.856, but gen-1 F1\,=\,0.036---the classifier almost entirely fails to identify first-generation Gemma continuations.
This is not a data-quality artifact: the Gemma-2-2B partition contains 4{,}957 instances with a balanced depth distribution ($\sim$990 per level).
A plausible explanation is that Gemma-2's first-generation continuations occupy a region of feature space highly similar to human-written text (gen-0), causing systematic misclassification of gen-1 as gen-0 or gen-2+.
This constitutes an architecture-specific generalization limitation rather than a systemic failure of the depth fingerprinting approach.

\paragraph{Scale effect.}
A clear parameter-count gradient emerges across the nine generators: small models ($\leq$1.7B) achieve F1\,$>$\,0.81, mid-range models (2--3B) cluster at 0.76--0.81, and large models (7B+) fall to 0.60--0.70.
Qwen3-8B (8.2B parameters) achieves 3-class F1\,=\,0.696 under the 9-gen split, compared to 0.714 in the 8-gen evaluation; this difference reflects the changed training composition (the 9-gen LOGO training set includes Gemma-2-2B data) rather than a property of the Qwen3-8B generator itself.

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

All eight generators are base (pretrained) models.
This is a deliberate design choice: base models isolate the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects, enabling controlled study of recursive distributional drift.
However, web text is predominantly produced by instruction-tuned and RLHF-aligned models.
Preliminary instruct experiments confirm that depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct drops to LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.763 base) and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template to 0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 under a 7-generator split).
Length-matched analysis yields near-zero correlations ($|\rho| < 0.02$) and binary classification near chance (F1\,$\approx$\,0.5) for Qwen models, leaving interpretation ambiguous.
Extending depth fingerprinting to instruct models requires addressing these confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping) that instruction tuning introduces.

Our experiments include generators up to 8.2B parameters (Qwen3-8B).
Depth signal persists at this scale (Qwen3-8B 3-class F1\,=\,0.714), but cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap vs.\ $\leq$2.8B generators (F1\,=\,0.77--0.81).
Frontier models (70B+) remain untested; their higher fluency may further compress feature margins.

Differential depth response strength is prompt-type dependent: within-type 3-class F1 ranges from 0.78 (continuation) to 0.73 (elaboration), with inspired rewriting intermediate at 0.74 (Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}).
DDR is most reliably detected in continuation-style generation; near-paraphrastic settings approach the method's detection floor.
Cross-prompt-type transfer (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753) confirms shared signal, yet additional prompt types (e.g., summarization, instruction following) and cross-generator $\times$ cross-prompt interactions remain untested.

Our primary evaluation uses single-generator chains; cross-model chains (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}) confirm depth signal under generator heterogeneity (3-class F1\,=\,0.789, binary F1\,=\,0.830; evaluated on the 5-generator subset for which cross-model chains were available), though these generators represent a controlled laboratory setting rather than the full diversity of real-world contamination.
Simulated human editing (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) suggests graceful degradation, but the gap between simulated token replacement and real-world post-processing remains untested.
Independent gen-0 seed sets per generator would eliminate potential memorization effects in 3-class LOGO evaluation; we report leak-free binary F1 as the primary metric to mitigate this limitation.

The reference model is fixed to Pythia-410M throughout, although cross-family reference experiments (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) confirm the phenomenon is not reference-specific (spread 0.013 across three references).
All seed texts in the main evaluation are English Wikipedia excerpts.
Cross-domain evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:domain}) shows that depth signal persists across News, Academic, and Code domains (binary F1 $>$ 0.73 under LOGO at $t{=}1.0$), though a domain $\times$ temperature interaction exists: certain domain/generator combinations at lower temperature approach chance level (e.g., Academic domain binary F1\,=\,0.628 at $t{=}0.7$), suggesting that reference model calibration is critical for cross-domain deployment.
The reference model dependency (Pythia-410M, English-centric pretraining) limits non-English applicability and adds inference overhead relative to surface-feature-only approaches.
Generalization to other languages remains untested.

Our default analysis uses fixed decoding parameters (temperature 0.7, nucleus $p{=}0.9$). A sampling ablation (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}) shows robustness to moderate variation ($t \in [0.5, 0.7]$, ${\leq}0.3$\,pp) but substantial degradation at $t{=}1.0$ ($-6$\,pp), indicating that depth fingerprinting assumes standard decoding regimes.
Cross-temperature transfer shows substantial degradation when test-time temperature exceeds training-time settings, limiting deployment to scenarios where the generation temperature is approximately known.

We use 3-class granularity (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+). A 5-class evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}) yields LOGO F1\,$\approx$\,0.50, with depths 2--4 mutually indistinguishable, validating the 3-class design as the practical resolution limit.
